papers.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

papers.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

papers.title: TutorCaseBench: A Case-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Tutors in Supporting Students with Challenging Behaviors
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used as AI tutors, yet existing benchmarks overlook the challenging behaviors common among students with learning and behavioral difficulties. We introduce TutorCaseBench, a benchmark that grounds AI-tutor evaluation in qualitative case studies from pedagogy, educational psychology, and special education. Our pipeline converts documented student categories into case-specific scenarios, tutor-student dialogues, and rubrics grounded in source evidence. The benchmark contains 923 dialogues across five challenge types, evaluated through open-ended response generation (1,560 items) and multiple-choice selection (2,537 items). Across 11 state-of-the-art LLMs, even the strongest model satisfies a rubric criterion in only 55.8% of open-ended cases, while models are better at selecting appropriate strategies than generating situated responses. These results reveal a gap between intervention recognition and context-specific adaptation, especially for open-weight models. All data are publicly available at https://github.com/kixlab/TutorCaseBench.

papers.title: Transparency Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Trust: Information Leakage and Procedural Overfitting in Supervised Machine Learning for Psychology
papers.abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

papers.title: Passing the Wrong Test: Model Size and Discriminant Validity in LLM-Based Psychological Assessment
papers.abstract: Validation studies of zero-shot language-model scoring of psychological interviews often rely primarily on a single convergent correlation with a questionnaire to establish validity. However, a bivariate correlation cannot reveal whether a model lacks discriminant validity, agrees poorly in absolute terms, produces non-random missing scores, or scores inconsistently. We evaluated eight open-weight families (1–70B active parameters) and eight commercial frontier models. The models scored the same sets of clinical interviews (Study 1: suicide recovery, n = 149; Study 2: future self-continuity, n = 164) across 52 configurations. Convergent validity improves with model size in both studies. However, the standard open-weight models tested achieve only about three-quarters of frontier convergent validity, with 11-fold greater mean absolute bias, more format failures, and lower repeatability in Study 1. In Study 2, standard open models (≤ 27B) are as strongly correlated with a closely related construct (suicide recovery) as with the target (mean difference −0.014), although they correlate less strongly with a distal neighbor (life satisfaction). All six frontier generations correlate more strongly with the target than with either neighbor (mean difference from recovery +0.117). On a local workstation, Gemma 4 31B is within the frontier range on all discriminant validity indices, outperforming its similar-sized predecessor. Llama 3.3 70B shows no greater discriminant validity than Gemma 4 31B, suggesting that discriminant validity is a function of release, not parameter count alone. Based on these findings, we suggest a minimum validation standard across five domains.

papers.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
papers.abstract: Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

papers.title: Dopaminergic reward signals shape foraging decisions through learned value expectations
papers.abstract: A fundamental function of the nervous system is to direct animals towards life-sustaining resources and enable adaptive strategies for acquiring them. Foraging, the challenge of securing these resources from the environment, requires making decisions that balance local gains against costs, opening a window on value-based decision making in ecological context. Yet despite the centrality of foraging in life, the algorithms and neural mechanisms underlying foraging decisions are not well understood. We studied mice making stay-or-leave patch foraging decisions for water across poor- and rich-resource environments with dynamic local reward outcomes. We found that mice integrate immediate rewards, local reward history, and reward (i.e. value) expectations to guide foraging decisions, favoring greater time investment in rich-environment patches. Computational models revealed influence of a time-varying bias which mirrored the shape of a learned value function. Consistent with a reinforcement learning mechanism, dopamine in the ventral striatum signaled a temporal-difference reward prediction error, which could be used as a teaching signal to construct value functions, and calibrated optogenetic manipulation of dopamine to create fictive reward signals recapitulated the value-related decision bias. Taken together, our results shed new light on the neurocomputational basis of foraging, revealing a novel role for value expectations in dynamic environments. Further, they establish generalized function of biological reinforcement learning in ecological context, demonstrating a specific role for the canonical dopamine reward circuit in shaping temporally resolved value expectations to guide behavior and cognition. The unification of this framework with foraging opens a new avenue to elucidate principles of how animals learn and dynamically adjust cognitive strategies for real-world ecological problems.

papers.title: Diagnosing the Explicit-to-Applied Theory of Mind Gap in LLMs
papers.abstract: As large language models are deployed in high-stakes roles such as therapy, education, and personal assistance, their social cognition must be assessed reliably. Current Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks report aggregate scores that conflate two distinct competencies: explicit ToM (recognizing what someone believes) and applied ToM (using that belief to predict behavior). Building on this distinction, we investigate the gap and its recoverability using four structurally diverse benchmarks. Aggregate reporting obscures uneven competence: on SimpleToM, Llama-3.1-8B scores 51.5 percent overall while recognizing mental states at 99.4 percent and predicting behavior at only 28.9 percent. papers.title: CoWriter: Guiding Methodological and Synergetic Human-LLM Co-Authoring

papers.title: Beyond Better Ideas: How Human-AI Collaboration Shapes Scientific Ideas and Human Perceptions
papers.abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.

papers.title: The Psychology of an AI Hacker

papers.title: Prefigured forgetting. Memory, the right to be forgotten and artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: This inaugural keynote lecture surveys the state of the art of the right to be forgotten and examines how it is being transformed by artificial intelligence. Drawing on cognitive science, philosophy and the social sciences, it treats forgetting as a constitutive function of memory, and recalls that remembering the past and imagining the future share the same mechanism. The core claim is that digital memory has moved through three regimes, archive, search engine and generative model, and that the right was designed for the first two. In the third, personal information is no longer stored as a locatable record but inferred and regenerated. Artificial intelligence prefigures the frameworks of individual and collective remembering. The right to be forgotten thus ceases to be merely an individual ex post remedy and becomes a property to be designed and governed within legal and ethical ecosystems along the artificial intelligence value chain.

papers.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
papers.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

papers.title: Testing the Translational Validity of the Learned Helplessness Model in Humans: Effects of Stressor Controllability on Reward Processing and Social Functioning
papers.abstract: Learned helplessness (LH) theory proposes that uncontrollable stress, but not otherwise identical controllable stress, produces behavioral consequences relevant to depression. Although extensively validated in animal models, the extent to which experimentally induced uncontrollability in humans reproduces depression-related behavioral alterations remains unclear. Here, we conducted one of the largest experimental investigations of human LH to date, using a preregistered yoked-control design in which participants were exposed to identical aversive stimuli but differed in their ability to control stimulus termination. We first examined whether uncontrollability impaired performance on a classic LH outcome measure, the anagram task. We then assessed its effects across multiple depression-relevant domains, including reward learning, effort-based reward motivation, and social behavior. Uncontrollability did not produce the broad behavioral impairments predicted by classical LH theory. Anagram performance showed effects in the expected direction but did not meet preregistered criteria for successful LH induction. Similarly, uncontrollability did not alter reward learning or social behavior, including social submissiveness and social avoidance. In contrast, uncontrollability selectively affected effort-based decision-making by reducing sensitivity to reward magnitude and probability when participants evaluated whether to exert effort for potential rewards. These findings suggest that acute experimentally induced uncontrollability in healthy adults does not produce a generalized depression-like behavioral syndrome but may selectively influence reward valuation processes underlying motivated behavior. More broadly, our results highlight the importance of identifying which components of depression-related dysfunction are reliably captured by laboratory models of stress controllability.

papers.title: Synthetic Selves for AI Agents? Lessons from Psychology for Agent-Based Modeling
papers.abstract: The growing interest in using large language models (LLMs) as human surrogates and as components of generative agent-based models (GABMs) raises a fundamental question for computational social science: what does it mean to model a person? The present paper surveys current work that uses LLMs to simulate human participants, with particular attention to their ability to reproduce findings of social psychology experiments. We document both the recurring challenges and the attempts to mitigate them. We then examine the possibility of endowing LLMs with a synthetic self by focusing on two psychological approaches to selfhood: trait-based personality and narrative identity. Our survey suggests that current LLM agents perform relatively well when selfhood is operationalized by rigidly structured means such as personality questionnaires, but are less reliable when it is induced by an unfolding narrative. We relate this problem to the characterization of LLMs as Decontextualized, Engineered, Anonymized, and Disembodies (DEAD) and consider its implications for GABMs. Drawing on the distinction between makeist and non-makeist takes on simulation, we argue that while GABMs may serve as a powerful tool for exploring how certain assumptions give rise to emergent phenomena, they do not necessarily constitute psychologically valid models of human behavior.

papers.title: Dynamic learning from good and bad outcomes peaks and persists in adolescence
papers.abstract: Learning good and bad associations and updating them amidst change facilitates adaptive behavior. Differences in sensitivity to salient, dynamic information from the environment may influence how learning unfolds. Cross-species research suggests that adolescents, relative to younger and older individuals, may exhibit more persistent learned negative and positive associations. However, direct within-person comparisons of valenced learning processes are scarce, and the mechanisms underlying developmental differences in the persistence of learned associations remain unclear. In adults, the persistence of negative associations has been linked to individual differences in how people use experience to infer the structure of their environment. Developmental changes in these same latent-structure inference processes may underpin greater persistence of valenced associations during adolescence. To test this, participants ages 10-25 years completed a Pavlovian learning task in which distinct cues predicted gain, loss, or neither, followed by extinction, during which outcomes ceased. Conditioned responses to both positive and negative associations peaked and took longer to extinguish in late adolescence, near age 19. Negative associations were similarly robustly learned in young adults and weakly persisted in a new extinction context in early adolescence. While a shared latent-structure inference process was observed across valences, age-related differences in the tendency to attribute changes in reinforcement contingencies to multiple latent states mirrored the persistence of valenced associations in adolescence. These findings suggest that while both positive and negative outcomes shape dynamic learning across age, valenced learned associations more strongly influence behavior and cognition during adolescence, as individuals learn to independently navigate a changing world.

papers.title: Bias and Reliability in Learning-Style Inference from Student--AI Dialogues: An Evaluation of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.

papers.title: BAIT: Can LLMs Find What Biases a Reader? A Benchmark for Cognitive Bias Triggers in News
papers.abstract: Persuasive writing exploits cognitive biases, recruiting a reader's mental shortcuts to shape belief, often without the reader noticing. We call the linguistic features exploiting such mental shortcuts cognitive bias triggers. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people encounter news, summarizing it, ranking it, and answering questions over it, a natural question is whether they can recognize the features of a text that bias a human reader. We introduce BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a resource for detecting cognitive bias triggers in news. BAIT pairs a schema of nine triggers, each specified in an annotator codebook, with 50 English news articles annotated by trained annotators at the article and span levels and adjudicated into a gold standard. On this data we define two tasks, detecting which triggers a text contains and locating the spans that carry them. We then benchmark six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples. The models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains, but rarely recover its full set of triggers, and they reach less than half of human agreement in locating the passages that carry them. Moreover, they over-predict triggers that come with easy surface cues, and most of the passages they mark for these triggers are not triggers, yet carry the trigger's surface cue far more often than random text. These findings suggest that the evaluated LLMs respond to surface cues rather than to the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative. We release the schema, the codebook, standoff annotations, and the evaluation pipeline.

papers.title: Conversational AI for Perceived Cognitive Decline Screening in Older Adults
papers.abstract: Early detection of cognitive decline in older adults remains challenging due to the resource demands of standard neuropsychological assessments. Chatbot-based Intelligent Cognitive Assistants (ICAs) provide a scalable alternative by eliciting open-ended responses rich in linguistic, semantic, and autobiographical cues. This study evaluates whether ICA question-answer (Q/A) interviews with older adults can screen for participant-reported perceived cognitive decline and related cognitive, functional, and personality outcomes. We compare traditional machine learning, frozen transformer embeddings, fine-tuned transformers, and large language model (LLM) reasoning strategies across Global Q/A, Single Q/A confidence averaging, and Aggregated Q/A pipelines. Among text-based methods, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (1-example-per-class, Aggregated Q/A) achieved the highest held-out test performance (0.742 accuracy, 0.739 balanced accuracy, 0.728 macro-F1). Given the small test set (n = 31), these results are interpreted descriptively. Frozen clinical transformer embeddings with a random forest head led non-LLM text methods, whereas fine-tuned models showed limited generalization. Models utilizing structured questionnaires, cognitive tasks, and personality traits outperformed text-based models in classification. Continuous regression analyses revealed modest predictive signals for AD8, FAQ, IQCODE, neuroticism, and conscientiousness. Exploratory prompt-level analyses identified both direct symptom-related and indirect autobiographical questions with strong test metrics, though sample sizes varied across prompts. These findings indicate that ICA chatbot interviews capture meaningful signals of perceived cognitive decline, supporting scalable screening research. Larger, clinically diverse cohorts with validated clinical outcomes are needed for clinical translation.

papers.title: Cognitive Maps in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Theory Unifying Value and Schema in the Prefrontal Cortex
papers.abstract: Animals exhibit behavioural flexibility by making reward-optimal decisions in unfamiliar situations. Computing value from minimal reward feedback requires leveraging known structure in the world. The Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) plays a pivotal role in both value computation and learning world structure, however mechanistic explanations for each---within the frameworks of Reinforcement Learning and Cognitive Maps---are largely distinct. We develop a mechanistic model of PFC that unifies value and structure through behavioural flexibility. In this model, value acts as a control signal that gates structured working memory representations of the current context in order to ultimately control behaviour. This is a significant departure from the conventional perspective of value, in which it is used for action readout. Critically, this model generalises to novel contexts without the need for additional synaptic plasticity. We demonstrate that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) meta-trained with either reinforcement learning or supervised learning recapitulate this exact model on various value-based tasks. These results not only provide a parsimonious explanation of both the value and schema frameworks of PFC function, but also propose a new mechanistic interpretation of the role of PFC in flexible decision making.

papers.title: Theta sequences support real-time spatial memory retrieval
papers.abstract: Oscillations play a critical role in orchestrating the timing of neural activity during cognitive processes. In the hippocampus, place cells encode spatial locations, and their activity is organized by theta oscillations into sequences that represent past, present, and potential future states. Recently, scrambling theta oscillations in vivo was shown to impair memory retrieval during navigation and decision-making, while leaving place cell activity intact. This surprising result highlights that the exact mechanisms underlying real-time memory encoding and retrieval in the hippocampus remain undefined. Here, we use a spiking neural network model of hippocampal theta sequences to evaluate the consequences of theta frequency scrambling on both representational learning and real-time spatial memory retrieval. We first show that frequency scrambling disrupts theta sequences and phase precession. Specifically, increased frequency scrambling was associated with a gradually degraded relationship between theta phase and spike timing, and ultimately abolished the predictive nature of place fields. When hippocampal spikes are required to solve a T-maze alternation task, the number of successful trials and navigation efficiency decreased with increasing values of frequency scrambling. These results could advance our understanding of how theta modulated neural activity supports memory-guided decision-making in real time and demonstrate why navigation fails when disrupting theta, despite intact spatial representations.

papers.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition

papers.title: Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains
papers.abstract: LLM planning research has traditionally focused on discrete-state domains, where actions form a finite, enumerable set. Existing LLM planning frameworks largely assume actions are enumerable, modeling planning as a search process over candidate actions. We find a remedy in Newell and Simon's Means-Ends Analysis (MEA), a general problem-solving technique rooted in heuristics from human psychology. We develop Medaka, an MEA-inspired structured prompting framework that encourages recursive goal decomposition, algebraic derivation, and per-step state tracking. To evaluate native LLM planning abilities in continuous-state domains, we develop Liquidworld, a systematic testbed on liquid mixing. On Liquidworld, Medaka can improve performance across model families, suggesting that classical means-ends analysis elicits LLM-native reasoning abilities that are helpful for continuous-state planning.

papers.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
papers.abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.

papers.title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure

papers.title: MOSS: A Production Framework for Monitoring and Diagnosing Semantic Failures in Search and Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract: Detecting semantic failures in production recommendation and search systems is hard: behavioral metrics lag by days, manual review does not scale, and most LLM evaluation frameworks are designed for offline, fixed datasets rather than continuous operational monitoring. We present Model Sanity Service (MOSS), a production framework that addresses this operational gap by embedding LLM-based relevance scoring into a recurring monitoring loop with targeted sampling, strategy-aware prompting, structured alerting, and diagnostic follow-up prompting that categorizes failures into actionable root causes. MOSS has been running in production at a large U.S. retailer for over six months across recommendation, search, and offer surfaces, and has surfaced two confirmed serving defects. For one of these, a backfill blending defect, MOSS quantified the impact of the proposed fix offline as a 76.4\% relative reduction in alert rate. On a 498-pair human-annotated recommendation benchmark, frontier LLM judges achieve higher F1 and AUC point estimates than non-LLM baselines (internal production embeddings and SBERT), with the largest gains on strategy-dependent tasks requiring intent-level relational reasoning. The same judge, score scale, and threshold transfer to a 466-pair search benchmark spanning 21 queries with only a surface-specific prompt adaptation, achieving strong F1 and AUC without retuning. These results show that a single LLM monitoring framework can provide useful, actionable quality signals across multiple product discovery surfaces in a large-scale e-commerce setting.

papers.title: From Trajectories to Differentiated Skills: Cognitive Differentiation for Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents tackle complex tasks through reasoning and interaction with external environments. Agent skills provide persistent, transferable capabilities that guide task planning, inform contextual decisions, support tool use, and enable executable procedures. Yet existing skill-evolution methods largely organize knowledge around skill artifacts, overlooking the functional heterogeneity within individual skills and its implications for knowledge maintenance and use. Inspired by cognitive science, we propose Cognitive Differentiation in Skill Evolution (CDSE), which evolves a unified skill through four functionally distinct yet coordinated components: Meta, Experience, Tool, and Script. CDSE extracts evidence-grounded semantic gradients from successful and failed trajectories, consolidates them by functional role, and applies component-specific updates and validation with cross-component coordination and adaptive invocation. An analysis of 500 top-ranked skill packages shows that 96.8% contain knowledge spanning at least two functional roles. Across six benchmarks, three agent models, and two execution harnesses, CDSE achieves the highest scores in all 36 settings, improving over the Base agent by 7.6 percentage points and the strongest competing method in each setting by 2.6 points on average. Ablation studies further support the importance of functional differentiation and adaptive invocation.

papers.title: EduWild: How Teacher-Configured Chatbots Fail in Real-World Use and How to Fix Them
papers.abstract: Teachers increasingly configure educational chatbots through natural-language instructions, but how these bots fail in real-world use remains poorly understood. We introduce EduWild, a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 teacher-configured chatbots, each paired with the instructions and configuration behind it, including 900 conversations from the intended end users of 35 deployed chatbots. We develop a 29-code taxonomy covering factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures and apply it using a human-calibrated LLM judge. The most frequent failures are lapses in following teacher intent --- bots skip required workflow steps (53.8% of end-user conversations), omit expectation setup (33.4%), and overload learners with information or questions (37.1%). Guided by these findings, we design a prompt-based harness targeting the six most frequent failure modes. In a study with 200 college students across ten bots, the harness reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation from 1.406 to 0.489, a 65.2% relative reduction with bots weighted equally. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbots.

papers.title: Designing Human-AI Collaborative Science: The 9A Framework
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human-AI collaboration offers a further mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments, and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human-AI coordination, and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. The organization layer specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). The coordination layer addresses how participants access relevant research information (Awareness), how scientific work advances through iterative proposal, execution, examination, revision, and resolution (Accountability), and when collaborative arrangements should be adjusted (Adaptability). The evaluation layer establishes what constitutes effective system performance (Achievement), how comparisons can be designed to identify the effects of organizational and coordination choices (Attribution), and what evidence supports the resulting conclusions (Assurance). Together, these layers frame HACS as a system-design problem, providing a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for empirically comparing their effectiveness.

papers.title: Cross-Centaur: Modeling Individual Decision-Making Across Psychological Tasks with Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human behavior. Recent models such as Centaur have advanced this goal by fine-tuning LLMs on trial-by-trial decisions from psychological experiments. However, existing large-scale behavioral datasets do not link the same participants across different tasks, so these models learn population-level regularities but are not trained to model individual-level regularities across tasks. We introduce Cross-Psych-101, a dataset of 591 participants and 261{,}551 valid decisions across 12 Bandit, Tradeoff, Structure, and Social tasks. We train Cross-Centaur to predict a participant's target-task actions from a target-task description and the source-task description paired with the same participant's source-task behavior. Cross-Centaur outperforms off-the-shelf LLMs and Centaur on held-out participants, both within and across tasks. Probing analyses suggest that its hidden states encode participant-level behavioral tendencies that transfer across tasks. These results highlight the potential of cross-task individual-level data for predicting human decision-making with language models. Cross-Pysch-101 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HikaruAsano/cross-psych-101.

papers.title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
papers.abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

papers.title: Emergent Discrimination and Polarization in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: We study theoretically how discrimination and polarization can emerge in a population of learning agents. Each agent uses an adaptive linear decision layer to map a language-model embedding of an issue to a binary opinion and maintains an evolving estimate of how much it trusts every other agent. Through pairwise interactions, agents update both their decision weights and trust estimates using an online Bayesian rule derived from teacher-student learning over a noisy channel. In-context-learning experiments with large language models qualitatively reproduce the predicted opinion and trust updates. We then assign each agent one of two arbitrary group labels, A or B, and model group bias by allowing a fraction $f_b$ of agents to shift its perceived agreement with each message by a strength $b$, a bias steering prejudice, depending on whether the sender and receiver share a label. We use order parameters from statistical mechanics to connect these local dynamics to collective states and transitions. Starting from uniformly random initial conditions, simulations reveal a rich phase diagram in the $(b,f_b)$ plane, comprising four collective states: spin-glass frustrated out-group favoritism, nondiscriminatory polarization, discrimination with opinion alignment, and discrimination without opinion alignment. Which state emerges depends on both the strength and prevalence of the bias. These results show how simple local learning dynamics can generate qualitatively distinct forms of polarization and discrimination, underscoring the need for population-level safety analysis of multi-agent systems. They also suggest measurable order parameters for characterizing analogous collective states in human societies.

papers.title: Dynamics of dopamine transients in human olfactory epithelium during reward learning
papers.abstract: Dopamine signaling is crucial for motivation, movement, and learning, but has remained beyond the reach of measurement in healthy humans. Here, we measured sub-second dopamine in the olfactory epithelium of healthy humans during two reward learning tasks with distinct reward types: liquid reward during a conditioning task and monetary reward during an economic exchange game. In both tasks, as trials progress, peak dopamine transients shift from rewarding outcomes back to reward-predictive cues. In the economic game, this pattern retrains quickly when reward magnitude or reward timing is changed without warning. These findings match the time transfer characteristics and amplitude dependence of temporal difference prediction error signals. The results also establish a new, minimally invasive route for recording fast dopamine signaling in healthy humans: the nose.

papers.title: Clustering of differential conditioned response trajectories using skin conductance: Are fear conditioning studies affected by pre-existing characteristics?
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that responses during experimental fear conditioning follow distinct latent trajectory classes. Computational reinforcement learning models can be used to infer latent learning processes during the task (e.g., learning rates and prediction-error sensitivity) that may help explain these classes. The present study re-analysed previously published and unpublished datasets to examine patterns of fear learning using skin conductance responses (SCRs) in a large sample of healthy participants. Data were aggregated from 12 fear conditioning experiments (N = 1,083; Mage = 20.72 years), encompassing acquisition, extinction, and return-of-fear phases. Using k-means clustering, we identified solutions comprising either two or three distinct response profiles. Across clusters, approximately half of participants showed minimal differential SCRs, while the remaining participants exhibited higher conditioned responding during acquisition, with subsets differing in whether fear returned following extinction. Cluster membership was significantly predicted by gender, current anxiety levels, post-acquisition conditioned stimulus pleasantness ratings, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for model-based learning. Comparison of reinforcement learning models indicated that a latent cause model provided a superior account of SCR data relative to Rescorla–Wagner, Pearce–Hall, and hybrid models, with latent cause parameters differing by cluster and gender. The clustering data provide preliminary evidence that SCR outcomes in fear conditioning studies may be disproportionately influenced by a minority of participants with specific pre-existing characteristics, rather than reflecting uniform learning processes. Moreover, the results provide support for latent cause theories of fear learning and highlight the value of combining clustering and computational approaches to better understand individual differences in fear acquisition, extinction, and relapse.

papers.title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.

papers.title: Brain-Aligned Multimodal LLMs for Social and Emotional Understanding of Cartoon Movies
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions. These findings support MLLMs as scalable tools for generating brain-predictive annotations of social and emotional content, while highlighting systematic rating differences and model- and stimulus-dependent alignment with human judgments.

papers.title: Using Language Models to Predict Values, Personality, Well-Being, and Meaning in Life From Ideal-Life Descriptions
papers.abstract: Does the way we picture our ideal life reveal what we value, who we are, and how we thrive? In a preregistered study (N = 273), we tested whether free-form descriptions (median 109 words) and seven-keyword lists of one's ideal life predict a broad battery of psychological constructs: the Big Five, the ten Schwartz values, social dominance, political orientation, meaning in life, and subjective well-being. Using regularized linear probes on embeddings from transformer large language models (LLMs), inspired by model-interpretability research, we find that ideal-life narratives predict most constructs above chance in both conditions (mean r = 0.24 for free-form, mean r = 0.12 for keywords). This free-form advantage was concentrated on constructs people rarely name outright, such as achievement, benevolence, conformity, and emotional stability, implying that part of the signal lies in the manner of the telling rather than in the referents alone. Nineteen of the 24 constructs were recovered from roughly 120 words of text, a far broader battery than earlier language-based work, which has relied on much longer samples and focused on personality and well-being. Our approach offers an open, privacy-preserving alternative to zero-shot commercial LLMs, with comparable accuracy, no API cost, and freely released data and code.

papers.title: Think Once, Reflect Twice: How Feedback Shapes Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making in high-stakes domains, designing effective human-AI collaboration becomes critical. Successful collaboration requires humans to reflect on decision-making processes and adjust their strategies accordingly. Current research typically investigates interventions, such as explainable AI, that target reflection during the decision-making process (reflection-in-action). Less attention has been given to retrospective examination of decisions (reflection-on-action). This work explores reflection-on-action by studying the impact of feedback on reliance behavior and human-AI team performance. Specifically, we investigate feedback interventions targeting overrides of AI advice through a behavioral study (N=244). We find that such feedback influences reflection-on-action, while unidirectional feedback risks reducing subsequent reflection-in-action. Furthermore, we identify opposing shifts in reliance behavior that leave overall human-AI team performance unchanged but show context-dependent effects. Balanced feedback did not show these risks, preserving both concurrent and retrospective reflection, offering insights for designing for appropriate reliance on AI.

papers.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
papers.abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

papers.title: Nicotinic control of dopamine release shapes striatal output and engages adaptive action selection.
papers.abstract: Acetylcholine and dopamine significantly modulate striatal circuits and are essential for reward learning and action selection. Cholinergic interneurons can locally trigger dopamine release through beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors expressed on dopamine axons1-3. However, the causal contribution of this local cholinergic control of dopamine to behaviour and striatal output remains unresolved, with recent studies reaching contrasting conclusions about the extent and behavioural relevance of local acetylcholine-dopamine coupling4-6. Here, to directly test the causal contribution of this pathway, we conditionally deleted beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptors from midbrain neurons in adult mice. This manipulation selectively abolished cholinergic interneuron-evoked dopamine release in the striatum. In a reward-based instrumental task, mice lacking this pathway showed decrements in effort that depended on the reinforcement context, and failed to adjust actions in a choice task when effort and reward costs varied. Substantia nigra beta2-containing nicotinic acetylcholine receptor deletion also markedly weakened cholinergic interneuron-mediated disynaptic inhibition of striatal projection neurons, showing that disruption of beta2-dependent cholinergic control of dopamine alters how cholinergic activity is transmitted to striatal output. Together, these findings establish the importance of local acetylcholine-dopamine coupling for regulating striatal output and influencing whether actions are sustained and adjusted as effort, reward, and outcomes change.

papers.title: Neural abstraction of evidence accumulation enables flexible multidimensional perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Human perceptual decisions adapt to rich and changing contexts but are typically tested under impoverished conditions. To probe this flexibility, we examined decisions requiring both the selection and the combination of multiple sensory features across sequences of objects. Here we show that human decision flexibility extends beyond feature selection to combination, even across sensory modalities, supported by the abstraction of underlying neural representations. Rapid magnetoencephalographic (MEG) responses reveal a hierarchy of object representations that become increasingly abstract and gated according to their decision relevance. A shared abstract representation of updates reflects evidence accumulation collapsed onto the relevant axis across unidimensional (selection-based) and multidimensional (combination-based) contexts. Recurrent neural networks tested under the same conditions acquire and benefit from abstract representations only when operating under human levels of computational noise. Together, these findings provide a flexibility through abstraction account of human decisions across a broader range of everyday perceptual conditions.

papers.title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
papers.abstract: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

papers.title: Integrating Simulation and Chain-of-thought Reasoning in Multimodal-Language Models For Physical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models often need to reason about the physical dynamics of the world in order to answer questions appropriately. Various methods have emerged for solving physical reasoning tasks, and in particular, two leading approaches are Chain-of-Thought reasoning and physics-grounded simulation. However, relatively little is known about which particular problems can be solved by each approach. Some tasks may benefit from computationally expensive generative video simulations, whereas others may be solved equally well (or even better) with language-based reasoning. Our work addresses this by systematically comparing simulation and language reasoning across a variety of multimodal tasks involving physical reasoning, such as answering questions about fluid dynamics and elasticity. We draw a parallel with this to resource-rational theories of human cognition, which propose that people optimally trade off simulation and reasoning depending on task demands. We present a novel cognitively-inspired hybrid model which optimally trades off simulation and reasoning to improve model performance and computational efficiency. Our model is able to decide the appropriate method to solve a physical reasoning problem at test time, and finds an optimal balance between accuracy and cost. Further, our model can be trained on a smaller vision-language model that is only 4B parameters and deployed to improve performance on much bigger base models with $>$3T parameters like Gemini 3 Pro.

papers.title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. We present AGORA (Agents Growing through Organization and Relational Arrangements), a framework that varies the two axes independently across three evolution mechanisms. Across web search, codebase understanding, and document QA, we find that (1) evolution alone rarely helps, while the right scaffolding surpasses a strong agent evolved alone by up to 25 points; (2) it does so by moving authority to the most capable member while the others step back; and (3) this member, having grown within the team, outperforms the same model alone. Designing a self-evolving MAS thus requires designing its social scaffolding, which shapes not only how its agents learn, but who gets to lead.

papers.title: Neuro-Symbolic Graph Transformers for Hierarchical Intention Recognition from Multimodal Human Activity Sequences
papers.abstract: Proactive human-robot collaboration requires autonomous systems to infer not only immediate actions but also the underlying hierarchical intentions governing human behavior. Current deep learning approaches predominantly focus on flat action classification, failing to capture the structural dependencies connecting kinematic motion to high-level goals. A Neuro-Symbolic Graph Transformer (NSGT) is proposed within this multimodal framework, a Human Reasoning Graph (HR-G) is integrated into the self-attention mechanism via learnable topological biases. Furthermore, the architecture is augmented with a differentiable First-Order Logic (FOL) loss, acting as a structural regularizer by which ontological consistency is enforced across four levels: atomic actions, composite activities, Low-Level Intentions, and High-Level Intentions. Evaluation is performed on the synthesized NTU-Hierarchy dataset, a four-level ontological extension of NTU RGB+D 120, wherein existing sequences were mapped into 119,383 complex hierarchical episodes (85 actions, 16 activities, 8 LLIs, 4 HLIs). To prevent circular supervision, strict isolation between label generation and FOL constraints was maintained. In the base configuration, 91.65% top-1 action accuracy is achieved by the NSGT. When the FOL loss is incorporated into the baseline, logic consistency is improved by 3.26 percentage points to 96.67%. Through the HR-G biases, a tunable trade-off between accuracy and structural coherence is established. In the primary consistency-maximizing configuration ($λ$ = 0.5), a logic consistency of 94.59% is reached and ontological contradictions are reduced by 33%, while a robust 89.90% top-1 action accuracy is retained. Finally, interpretable reasoning evidence is provided by the learned HR-G weights, wherein transition edges are strongly exploited ($β$ trans $\approx$ +2.6) without explicit supervision.

papers.title: Making AI-mediated decisions culturally repairable
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly influences high-stakes decisions, from employment and education to healthcare and public services. When such judgments are disputed, affected people may receive an explanation without being able to reach an authority empowered to change the outcome or remedy its consequences. We introduce cultural repairability: the institutional capacity to review an AI-mediated decision, correct the outcome and downstream records, provide meaningful restoration, and learn from failure through procedures people can understand and use. The framework addresses a visibility–accountability asymmetry: people are exposed to judgments about their standing but lack effective means of obtaining an answer or remedy. Culture matters because exposure, legitimate authority, and appropriate restoration may be understood differently across settings. Language accessibility also determines whether review mechanisms are usable in practice. We identify three measurable cultural mechanisms: the meaning of exposure, the credibility of review, and the meaning of restoration. We further distinguish affected people’s appraisals from institutional actors’ responsibility and capacity to respond. Four falsifiable propositions specify how reviewer authority and audience shape responses to repair, and how these effects vary with cultural orientation, institutional history, and the form of restoration. They predict whether people appeal or withdraw, how they recalibrate trust, and whether they remain willing to engage. The resulting Repairability Principle establishes a common floor of substantive review, correction, restoration, and prevention of recurrence, while allowing people to choose how restoration is delivered. Cultural repairability therefore shifts global AI accountability from whether procedures appear acceptable to whether institutions can correct harm in practice.

papers.title: Machine--human agreement in marking undergraduate assignments is specific to model, prompt and institution
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) promise to automate one of higher education's most resource-intensive activities: assessing student writing. Existing evaluations are typically limited to a single model, a single prompt and a single institution. Using 761 undergraduate psychology assignments from three UK universities, we evaluated three frontier LLMs, individually and in ensemble, on accuracy, prompt sensitivity, error independence, generalisability and evidential basis. Agreement between human and machine marks varied widely, with no model or prompt optimal across institutions. All models compressed marks towards a common central tendency, overvaluing the weakest assignments and undervaluing the strongest. Because this error was shared, ensembling failed to remove it. Machine marks also rewarded linguistic features more strongly than human marks. Since human-machine agreement was a joint product of model, prompt and institution, we conclude that current LLMs lack evaluative capacity transferable across contexts, and that single-context validation overstates readiness for deployment.

papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

papers.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
papers.abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.

papers.title: Beyond Belief Nesting: Rethinking Higher-Order Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.

papers.title: Calibrating LLM Explanations to Human Decisions with Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Explanations of LLM outputs are considered an important way to make model behavior legible, helping human users make good decisions on downstream tasks. However, default training approaches for improving explanations target model task performance or human preference rather than human decision quality. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textbf{HD-RL}, a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing LLM explanations for human decision making. Our approach calibrates a human decision simulator on observed human decisions, applying a proxy reward model to optimize the LLM to generate explanations that help people to make good decisions. We apply this framework to AI-generated text detection. In our initial data collection phase, we observed that while LLMs possess strong autonomous detection capabilities, the explanations they generate for users yield near-random human accuracy (51.3\%). By applying the HD-RL framework to the open-source Qwen 3.6 model, we generate optimized explanations that improve human performance, achieving a GLMM-estimated human accuracy of 63.7\% in a randomized between-subjects experiment with repeated measures and outperforming RLVR, RLAIF, and other baselines by over 8\%.

papers.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human-machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human-computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human-machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

papers.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
papers.abstract: Psychological scales designed for humans are increasingly administered to language models, and differences between their responses in two languages are read as evidence of cultural tendency. Such comparisons presuppose that the two language versions measure the same thing. This study tests that premise. Three established social orientation scales were administered to four models built by United States and Chinese developers in Chinese and English under two temperature settings. Responses were then decomposed, using a psychometric model that separates a latent trait from a directional response bias, into the component that tracks what the instrument is meant to measure and the component that does not. The cross-linguistic difference is not one quantity. On scales with balanced keying, every estimate showed a higher trait and a lower bias under Chinese prompting, the bias moving further than the trait in most conditions. Because the two components run in opposite directions, they offset one another on scales containing no reverse-keyed items, where they also cannot be separated. A difference reported on such a scale therefore does not establish that models differ in the construct, only that they answered differently. Two further manipulations show that the difference is produced by item wording, though not by negation, and that the stability of a model identifier over four weeks varies by an order of magnitude between vendors. We set out three checks that would make cross-linguistic comparison interpretable: balanced keying, decomposition to the item level, and a contemporaneous control whenever collections are compared across time.
